t: #3017 Count the Number of Houses at a Certain Distance II
o: Houses 1..n form a path, plus one extra edge between x and y (possibly a self-loop when x = y). For each k we must count ordered pairs at shortest-path distance exactly k. With n up to 1e5, BFS from every house (O(n^2)) is too slow; we exploit the structure. The extra edge creates a cycle spanning houses min(x,y)..max(x,y). Distances shrink only for pairs whose straight-line path crosses the whole cycle or benefits from the chord; all other pairs keep path distance |i - j|. In example 2 (n=5, x=2, y=4) the cycle 2-3-4-2 shortens pairs like (1,4): min(3, 1+1+0)=2.
k: Split houses into three regions: left of the cycle [1, mn-1], the cycle [mn, mx], and right [mx+1, n], where mn = min(x,y), mx = max(x,y).
Within the cycle, distance is min(|i-j|, L-|i-j|) with L = mx-mn+1 (ring metric).

Cross-region distances are minima of the straight route and the chord route; for each fixed endpoint these minima switch at most once, so contributions form contiguous ranges of k — perfect for a difference array.
Ordered pairs mean every unordered pair contributes 2.

a.n: Approach 1: BFS from every node (conceptual baseline)
a.i: Run BFS from each house over the n+1 edges and bucket the resulting distances. Trivially correct but O(n^2) time — only viable to explain the problem or for tiny n; included to motivate the counting solution.
s: Build adjacency: path edges i—i+1 plus edge x—y (skip if x == y).
BFS from each source, incrementing ans[d] for each reached distance d.
a.t: O(n^2) — one O(n) BFS per source; too slow for n = 1e5 in the worst case
a.sp: O(n) for adjacency and distance arrays

a.i: Let mn = min(x,y), mx = max(x,y), L = mx-mn+1, g = mx-mn-1. Count ordered pairs by category, adding each category's distance multiset as O(1) range updates on a difference array over k: (1) left-left and right-right pairs contribute ordinary path distances; (2) intra-cycle pairs contribute ring distances; (3) left-cycle pairs have d = min(j-i, mn-i+1+mx-j), which switches once as j grows, giving two arithmetic ranges per i; (4) right-cycle pairs symmetrically; (5) left-right pairs always take the chord route, d = j-i-g, again a range per i. A final prefix sum materializes the answer. Handle x == y separately (plain path).
s: Special-case x == y: answer is 2*(n-k) for each k.
Add left-left and right-right contributions 2*(regionSize - d) for each d, and ring contributions 2L (or L for the diametric case when L is even) per distance d ≤ L/2.
For each left node i add ranges [mn-i, t-i] and [mn-i+1, mn-i+mx-t] (t = floor((mn+mx+1)/2)); mirror for right nodes; add [mn+2-i, n-i-g] for left-right pairs.
Prefix-sum the difference array into the result.
a.t: O(n) — a constant number of difference-array updates per house, then one prefix-sum pass
a.sp: O(n) for the difference array and answer

w: Present BFS as the correctness baseline, then derive the counting solution — interviewers want the region decomposition and the 'minimum switches once, so ranges' argument. Pitfalls: mishandling x == y (self-loop changes nothing), x and y adjacent (g = 0, chord is redundant), the diametric ring case contributing L not 2L, and off-by-one boundaries in the range updates — validate against all three examples. Follow-up: multiple extra edges (then BFS multi-source or 01-BFS tricks), or answering queries for specific pairs online.
